Sputnik 1. The Soviet Union launched the first artificial satellite on October 4, 1957, beginning the Space Age and the Space Race. Sputnik was a polished metal sphere about 58 centimetres in diameter, with four external radio antennas. The name Sputnik means traveling companion in Russian; the full name was Sputnik Zemlya, or Earth Satellite.

The satellite orbited Earth every 96 minutes and transmitted simple radio beeps on two frequencies that radio operators worldwide could detect. It lasted three weeks before its batteries were depleted, though it remained in orbit for three months before burning up on re-entry.

The launch shocked American leadership and the public. It sparked the Space Race and intensified Cold War anxieties about Soviet technological superiority. Sputnik's success prompted the creation of NASA in 1958 and shifted American education and science funding dramatically. The West had suddenly fallen behind, or at least that was how it seemed. A satellite circling overhead, a beeping reminder of Soviet achievement, transformed how Americans thought about technology and science. It galvanized the nation in ways that still reverberate today in how we fund research and educate scientists.
